title: The Place and Role of Philosophy in the Islamic World in the Formation of Medieval European Philosophy
content: The contribution of philosophy in the Islamic world to medieval European thought extends beyond the preservation and transmission of ancient Greek texts. This article examines the interpretative, conceptual, and intellectual roles of Muslim philosophers in the formation of European philosophical traditions, with particular attention to al-Fārābī, Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), and Averroes (Ibn Rushd). Adopting a historical and comparative approach, the study considers the translation movements through which ancient and Arabic-language philosophical works circulated, the reception of Islamic philosophical concepts within Latin scholasticism, and the emergence of Averroism in the European university environment. Particular attention is given to the engagement of Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas with Arabic philosophy, alongside the debates associated with Siger of Brabant and the University of Paris. The article argues that thinkers of the Islamic world functioned as active producers of philosophical knowledge whose commentaries, critical analyses, and original theories helped reshape the intellectual resources available to European scholars. Their reception also generated disputes concerning the authority of Aristotle, the relationship between reason and revelation, and the scope of philosophical inquiry. By distinguishing intellectual transmission from conceptual transformation, the study presents medieval European philosophy as developing through sustained engagement across linguistic, religious, and cultural boundaries.
